684: Third, Kapp (1987) reports a few isolated cases involving centralization of back vowels
685: before retroflex consonants in Alu Kurumba. Muduga also has some cases of this kind, often
686: involving the same words. A few examples are listed in Table 19. The Kodagu cognates do
687: not exhibit centralization, but those of Alu Kurumba do, suggesting that the exceptions in
688: Muduga and Alu Kurumba might share a common origin.

699: Fourth, retracted *i has merged with unrounded *u in Kodagu (Emeneau 1970), as in
700: Muduga, but not in Irula or Alu Kurumba. However, it is not clear if this reflects an empirical
701: difference between the languages, or different analytical choices. Even in Muduga, it might
702: be possible to treat [ɨ] and [ɯ] as allophones of /u/ outside of initial root syllables.
703: Vowel retraction in Muduga, Alu Kurumba, Irula, and Kodagu, most likely reflects a
704: shared innovation or areal feature, with minor variations in each language. As mentioned,
705: there are unconfirmed reports of related developments in other South Dravidian languages
706: (see Section 1). Moreover, similar patterns of retraction have been reported at the subphonemic level in various dialects of Tamil, including those of Madurai (Zvelebil 1960),
707: Dindigul (Zvelebil 1961), Erode (Zvelebil 1963), Ramnad (Zvelebil 1963), and Jaffna in Sri
708: Lanka (Kuno 1958). Allophonic centralization also occurs in some varieties of Kannada
709: (Učida et al. 2013: xi), and we have heard it in the Kasaragod dialect of Malayalam. These
710: sub-phonemic cases likely represent further examples of the same general development
711: which have not achieved phonemic status.
712: Toda has also retracted short *i to /ɯ/ (or /ɨ/), but the change was not conditioned by
713: retroflexes. Rather, it reflects the default development of PDr short *i in most environments.
714: Moreover, long *iː has been preserved without retraction, even before retroflexes 20
715: (Subrahmanyam 1983). Thus, there is no relation between vowel retraction in Toda and
716: vowel retraction in Muduga, or any of the other languages cited above.
718: While there are numerous reports of vowel retraction in South Dravidian, there are few
719: reports of vowel fronting before alveolars or palatals. The clearest parallel to Muduga is the
720: dialect of Irula described by Diffloth (1968). In this dialect, all back vowels, including short
721: and long *u, *o, and *a, have been fronted before alveolars (but not palatals). In polysyllabic
722: words, word-final alveolar *n was dropped, leaving fronted [æ] in word-final position with
723: no apparent conditioning factor, exactly as in Muduga. Zvelebil’s (1971) description of Irula
724: included rounded and unrounded centralized vowels (/y, ɯ, ø, ɤ/, short and long), but made
725: no mention of /æ/. Zvelebil expressed uncertainty about the rounding feature and its source
726: with respect to centralized vowels in Irula. He suggested that some central round vowels
727: might derive from *u before a front vowel in the following syllable (1971: 121). In the
728: examples cited, however, the fronted vowels occur before alveolars. Thus, it is possible that
729: Zvelebil’s informants exhibited the same pattern that Diffloth observed, but Zvelebil did not
730: notice the conditioning effect of alveolars.
731: A comparable case of fronting has been reported in Parji, a Central Dravidian language of
732: Chhattisgarh. In Parji, PDr *a and *aː have become /e/ and /eː/ before alveolar consonants,
733: but other back vowels have not been affected (Krishnamurti 1978; Subrahmanyam 1983).
734: The change of *a to /e/ before alveolars clearly resembles the fronting of *a in Muduga and
735: Irula. However, there is an important difference. In Parji, fronting resulted in the merger of
736: *a and *e before alveolars, whereas in Muduga and Irula, it results in a new vowel quality,
737: /æ/, which stands in contrast with /e/. Parji is not close to Muduga and Irula, genetically or
738: geographically. Thus, fronting before alveolars might represent a shared innovation or areal
739: trait for Muduga and Irula, but it probably represents an independent development in Parji.
740: Other cases of fronting are reported in Kota and Toda but their conditioning factors are
741: different, and they do not appear related (Subrahmanyam 1983). Tamil, Malayalam, and
742: Kannada, all have /æ/ as a marginal phoneme in English loanwords (Annamalai and Steever
743: 1998; Asher and Kumari 1997; Sridhar 1990), but they do not exhibit fronting of *a in native

773: Various descriptive terms have been applied to vowels that have evolved under the influence
774: or retroflex consonants, including terms like retroflex or rhotacized, on the one hand, and
775: retracted or centralized, on the other. There are correlations among these terms, but they are
776: not necessarily equivalent. Retroflexion is a gesture in which the tongue tip is turned up or
777: curled back, typically resulting in an apical or sub-apical articulation in the post-alveolar or
778: palatal region. Retraction refers to displacement of the tongue dorsum toward the velum or
779: pharynx, as in secondary velarization or pharyngealization. In principle, these two gestures
780: are distinct. In practice, however, retroflexion is often accompanied by retraction (Bhat 1974;
781: Hamann 2002, 2003). As a result, a phonological correlation between retroflexion and back
782: vowels can be observed in many languages (e.g., Lin 1989; Gnanadesikan 1994; Hamann
784: Retroflex consonants tend to exert more influence on preceding vowels than following
785: vowels. This can be attributed to the dynamic nature of retroflex articulations. The tongue tip
786: is curled back (and the tongue body potentially retracted) for the onset of a retroflex segment,
787: but it can move forward during production and be released toward the anterior part of the oral
788: cavity. This property of retroflexion is sometimes called flapping-out (Bhat 1973; Hamann
789: 2003). The curling of the tip and retraction of the body can begin early, during the preceding
790: vowel. As a result, retroflex consonants tend to have strong co-articulatory and perceptual
791: effects on preceding vowels, as witnessed in Muduga and other South Dravidian languages.
792: However, due to flapping-out, there is little or no tongue curl or retraction at the time of
793: release. Thus, they tend to have little effect on following vowels (Steriade 2001).
794: Recall that rhotacized vowels can be retroflex or bunched, but the two articulations are
795: virtually indistinguishable acoustically (Section 4.3). Given the correlations between
796: retroflexion, rhotacization, and retraction, it is no surprise that different terms are often
797: applied interchangeably to vowels that come under the influence of retroflex consonants.
798: Nevertheless, retraction of front vowels (resulting in centralization) can and should be
799: distinguished from rhotacization, whether retroflexed or bunched. Our study indicates that
800: Muduga /ɯ/ and /ɤ/ are retracted in relation to PDr *i and *e, from which they evolved, and 22
801: centralized relative to other vowels in the system, but they are not rhotacized (retroflex or
802: bunched). This is not a foregone conclusion. Kalasha, an Indo-Aryan language of the Dardic
803: group in northern Pakistan, has rhotic vowels that evolved under the influence of retroflex
804: consonants, much like the vowels of Muduga (Heegård and Mørch 2004). The rhotic vowels
805: are somewhat centralized relative to their non-rhotic counterparts but, unlike Muduga, they
806: are clearly rhotacized with substantially lower F3 values (Kochetov et al. 2019, 2021;
807: Hussain & Mielke 2021). Moreover, Badaga, a South Dravidian language related to Muduga,
808: was reported to have retroflex vowels that developed under the influence of PDr *ɻ and *ɭ
809: (Emeneau 1939). The vowels are lost in contemporary dialects (Hockings and Pilot-Raichoor
810: 1992), but Peter Ladefoged and associates recorded some speakers in the early 1990s (cf.
811: Ladefoged and Maddieson 1996: 314). We have examined their field recordings and found
812: that the vowels are clearly of the retroflex/rhotic type (with low F3), like Kalasha, not the
813: retracted/centralized type, like Muduga (Arsenault 2022). Thus, both retroflex/rhotacized and
814: retracted/centralized vowels can evolve under the influence of retroflex consonants, and both
815: developments are attested in South Dravidian. Badaga is of the former type, while Muduga is
816: of the latter type. Irula, Alu Kurumba, and Kodagu appear to be more like Muduga, but
817: studies are needed to confirm their phonetic properties.
818: The affinity between front vowels and palatal or laminal post-alveolar consonants is wellestablished cross-linguistically and needs no comment (Bhat 1978, Bateman 2007). However,
819: the fronting influence of alveolars in Muduga and Irula is interesting, especially given that
820: dentals are inert. This topic warrants further investigation. For the present, we hypothesize
821: that alveolars might be produced with a fronted tongue body to enhance their contrast with
822: the retroflex series. Given that both alveolar and retroflex consonants are apical (articulated
823: with the tongue tip), they might be distinguished primarily by tongue body positions, as
824: suggested for /ɾ/ and /r/ in Malayalam (Scobbie et al. 2013). We leave this question for future
827: Our study contributes to the documentation of Muduga, a minority language that has received
828: little attention in comparative Dravidian studies to date. It confirms the development of
829: centralized vowels in Muduga, thereby resolving one of several disputed cases of innovative
830: vowels in South Dravidian. Specifically, the study affirms that the innovative vowels of
831: Muduga are centralized along the front-back axis in relation to inherited front and back
832: vowels. They are not rhotacized (retroflex or bunched), like the vowels of Kalasha or Badaga,
833: despite having similar historical origins. More studies are needed to confirm the occurrence
834: of innovative vowels in other South Dravidian languages, and to clarify the phonetic nature
835: of the vowels where they occur.

534: Given that vowel retraction has been conditioned by retroflex consonants and /r/, we also
535: examined F3 values to see if the retracted vowels show any sign of retroflexion or
536: rhotacization. Rhotic vowels can be produced in one of two ways. Either the tongue tip is
537: turned up toward the palate while the tongue body is lowered (and possibly retracted) or the
538: tongue tip is down with the body raised toward the palate and bunched along the anteriorposterior axis (Ladefoged and Maddieson 1996; Ladefoged and Johnson 2015). The first of
539: these articulations (tip up) can be classified as retroflex while the second (tip down) is often
540: described as a bunched rhotic. Both strategies yield similar acoustic results, and speakers
541: might use either strategy to produce the same vowels (Delattre and Freeman 1968; Mielke et
542: al. 2016). The most consistent acoustic property of rhotacization, whether retroflex or
543: bunched, is a dramatic lowering of F3 (Ladefoged and Maddieson 1996; Hamann 2003).
544: Front vowels typically have higher F3 values relative to central and back vowels. Thus,
545: any retraction of front vowels is expected to yield lower F3 values even without
546: rhotacization. Rhotacization, by comparison, is expected to yield F3 values that are
547: substantially lower than those of regular central and back vowels. Compare the mean formant
548: values of Korean central [ɨ], in Figure 4, with those of American English rhotacized [ə˞], in
549: Figure 5. Korean [ɨ] has one of the lowest F3 values in the language, but its F3 is still in the
550: range of 2500 Hz for male speakers, which is not much different than [a] or [u]. In contrast to
551: this, English [ə˞] has F3 values in the range of 1800 Hz for male speakers, which is
552: substantially lower than the F3 values of any other vowel in the system, including those of
553: other central and back vowels. Thus, if Muduga /ɯ/ and /ɤ/ are rhotacized, we should expect
554: them to have very low F3 values comparable to English [ə˞] in Figure 5; but if they are
555: retracted without rhotacization, we should expect them to have F3 values comparable to other
556: central or back vowels, like Korean [ɨ] in Figure 4. 15

603: retracted *i and unrounded *u have merged in the phoneme /ɯ/.

624: and (relatively) front rounded [y, ø]. On average, they are more central than front; they rarely

629: In summary, acoustic evidence indicates that /ɯ/ and /ɤ/ are central or back-central
630: unrounded, but not retroflex or rhotacized, while /æ/ is front-central unrounded, and the
631: fronted allophones of /u/ and /o/ are central or front-central rounded. In the following section,

17: Abstract: Proto-Dravidian had a system of ten vowels consisting of five qualities (i, e, a, o,
18: u), each with short and long counterparts. Some South Dravidian languages have expanded
19: systems with innovative vowels that are described as centralized or retroflex. However, the
20: phonetic nature of the vowels, and the list of languages that have them, remain poorly
21: defined. We present evidence that Muduga, a South Dravidian language of Kerala, is among
22: the languages with expanded vowel systems. It has five innovative vowel qualities, three of
23: which can be considered phonemic. Historical-comparative evidence indicates that the new
24: qualities result from: (i) retraction of front vowels before retroflex consonants and alveolar
25: /r/; and (ii) fronting of back vowels before alveolar and palatal consonants (except /r/ and /j/).
26: Loss of conditioning consonants in some contexts has led to emergent contrasts. Acoustic
27: phonetic analysis of two male speakers suggests that the new vowels are centralized along the
28: front-back axis, but not retroflex or rhotacized. We compare these results to related
29: developments in other South Dravidian languages and discuss correlations between
30: retroflexion and retraction that motivate the observed patterns.

35: Proto-Dravidian (PDr) had a system of ten vowels consisting of five qualities (i, e, a, o, u)
36: with short and long counterparts (Subrahmanyam 1983; Krishnamurti 2003). This system is
37: preserved with few changes in most Dravidian languages. However, some South Dravidian
38: languages have innovative vowels described variously as centralized, back unrounded,
39: retracted, or retroflex. These vowels are found in a relatively contiguous group of languages
40: spoken in the Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu and adjacent parts of Kerala and Karnataka,
41: leading some to speculate that “a variety of centralized (or retroflexed) vowels” might
42: constitute an areal feature of that region (Diffloth 1975: 55).
43: Unfortunately, the picture of centralized vowels in Dravidian remains sketchy. It is not
44: entirely clear which languages have the vowels and which do not. They are best documented
45: in Toda (Emeneau 1957), Kodagu (Emeneau 1970), Irula (Diffloth 1968; Zvelebil 1971), and
46: Alu Kurumba (Kapp 1987), but there are conflicting reports for Badaga (Emeneau 1939; cf.
47: Hockings and Pilot-Raichoor 1992), Betta Kurumba (Zvelebil 1982; cf. Coelho 2003), and
48: Muduga (Rajendran 1986; cf. Kapp 1987). There have been tentative reports of centralized
49: vowels in Palu Kurumba (Kapp 1978), Jennu Kurumba (Zvelebil 1980, 1988), Sholaga
50: (Zvelebil 1990), and Urali (Lal 1991), but there have been no follow up studies to shed
51: further light on those cases. Moreover, even where the centralized vowels are best
52: documented, their phonetic properties are not always clear. Most of the studies were
53: conducted before the tools of acoustic phonetics were accessible to field workers. Thus, the
54: studies were purely impressionistic. A wide range of phonetic symbols and descriptive terms
55: have been applied to the vowels, making it hard to tell if we are dealing with the same vowels
56: under different labels or different vowels in each language.
57: This paper examines the case of centralized vowels in Muduga, a South Dravidian
58: language of Kerala. Rajendran (1986) described Muduga as having a classic Dravidian vowel
59: system with five qualities and contrastive length. He made no mention of centralized vowels.
60: However, citing his own unpublished fieldnotes, Kapp (1987) listed Muduga among the
61: languages with centralized vowels. We present historical and acoustic evidence supporting
62: Kapp’s (1987) observation. Specifically, we demonstrate that Muduga has developed two
63: back-central unrounded vowel qualities, /ɯ/ and /ɤ/, through the retraction of front vowels
64: before retroflex consonants and /r/. The loss of conditioning consonants in some
65: environments has promoted these vowels to phonemic status. Acoustic evidence indicates
66: that they range between central and back unrounded, but they are not retroflex or rhotacized,
67: despite their diachronic origin. In addition, we demonstrate that Muduga has developed three
68: other qualities, [y], [ø], and [æ], through the fronting of back vowels before alveolar and
69: palatal consonants (except /r/ and /j/). Of these, only /æ/ has achieved phonemic status, while
70: [y] and [ø] can be treated as front-central allophones of /u/ and /o/, respectively. The net
71: result is a system of sixteen vowel phonemes, consisting of eight qualities (five inherited,
73: Our study contributes to the documentation of an under-studied minority language and, in
74: so doing, confirms another case of centralized vowels in South Dravidian. Moreover, it
75: provides an empirically grounded description of the vowels based on acoustic phonetic
76: evidence. To our knowledge, no acoustic studies of centralized vowels in Dravidian have 2
77: been published to date. The present study is a first step toward filling this gap and addressing
78: the lack of clarity in phonetic descriptions.
79: The paper is organized as follows. We begin with an introduction to Muduga in Section 2.
80: We then present historical-comparative evidence of vowel retraction and fronting (Section 3),
81: followed by an acoustic phonetic analysis of the vowel system (Section 4). In Section 5, we
82: relate the results of our study to previous research on centralized vowels in Dravidian. In
83: Section 6, we discuss the correlations between retroflexion and retraction that motivate many
84: of the diachronic developments. Finally, we offer some concluding remarks in Section 7.
86: The Muduga (or Mudugar) are a scheduled tribe of India consisting of approximately 3000–
87: 3500 people living in the Attappady block of Mannarkkad Taluk in Palakkad district of
88: Kerala state (Varghese 2015). Map 1 shows their location, which borders on the Nilgiri and
89: Coimbatore districts of Tamil Nadu. The name Muduga refers to both the people and their
90: language, which is classified as South Dravidian (Eberhard et al. 2021). Unfortunately, the
91: Muduga language remains under-documented and has not figured in comparative Dravidian
92: studies to date. Thus, its precise place within the South Dravidian group has not been
93: determined. It has been identified as a dialect of Tamil (Luiz 1962) or possibly Kannada
94: (Menon 1996). However, Rajendran (1986) has argued that it has sufficient lexical and
95: morphological differences to consider it a distinct language, and the International
96: Organization for Standardization has assigned it a unique three-letter code in the ISO 639-3

100: Malayalam is the official state language of Kerala and functions as the language of wider
101: communication in Palakkad district, where Muduga is spoken. Across the state border, these
102: functions are filled by Tamil. Most Muduga speakers use Malayalam as a second language,
103: and some are also proficient in Tamil. The Muduga people live in close contact with two
104: other scheduled tribes in Attappady block: the Irula and Kurumba. They associate most
105: closely with the Kurumba, with whom they often intermarry (Rajendran 1986). The Irula and
106: Kurumba speak their own varieties of South Dravidian, and both have communities with
107: related dialects on the Tamil Nadu side of the border.

120: A few points about the consonant system are worth noting. First, like Malayalam and a
121: few other South Dravidian varieties, Muduga preserves the PDr distinction between dental,
122: alveolar, and retroflex stops in word-medial geminates. Secondly, it also maintains the
123: contrast between retroflex and non-retroflex nasals and laterals. Thirdly, it has two distinct
124: rhotics: a laminal alveolar flap or tap /ɾ/, and an apical alveolar trill /r/. These have distinct
125: historical sources and phonological behaviours. The tap /ɾ/ is a reflex of PDr *r and patterns
126: phonologically with other alveolars, such as /l/ and /n/. The trill /r/ is a reflex of PDr alveolar
127: *t, but it patterns phonologically with the retroflex series (as a trigger of vowel retraction),
128: not with alveolars (as a trigger of vowel fronting). On historical and distributional grounds,
129: alveolar [t], [d], and [r] can be considered allophones of a single phoneme, corresponding to
130: PDr *t: [t] occurs in medial geminates, [d] occurs after nasals, and [r] occurs elsewhere.
131: However, given their distinct phonological behaviours, we tentatively treat /t/ (with [d] as an
132: allophone) and /r/ as marginally distinct phonemes.1 Fourthly, [s] is a reflex of PDr *c and
133: can be considered an allophone of /ʧ/ word-initially.2 Finally, [n̪], [ɲ], and [ŋ] can be
134: considered allophones of /n/ occurring before homorganic stops.

154: Vowel length is phonemic for all vowel qualities, but the contrast is neutralized wordfinally in polysyllabic words. Final vowels tend to be phonetically long when words are
155: uttered in isolation, but short otherwise. They are treated as phonemic short vowels with
156: predictable length in final position. Nasalization is not phonemic. All vowels are nasalized
157: after nasal consonants, but not notably before them.
158: In the following sections, we explore the historical development of Muduga vowels and
159: their phonetic properties in greater detail. Our study is concerned primarily with vowel
160: quality independent of length. To simplify the presentation, we avoid specifying length
161: wherever the point at hand applies to both short and long vowels. Unless stated otherwise, a
162: reference to PDr *i or Muduga /ɯ/ should be interpreted as a reference to the specified
163: quality, including both its short and long counterparts. For instance, if we say that PDr *i
164: corresponds to Muduga /ɯ/ in some context, the reader should understand that we mean short
165: *i corresponds to short /ɯ/, while long *iː corresponds to long /ɯː/ in that context. Where
166: length distinctions are relevant, they are made explicit.

193: The results of our historical-comparative study indicate that the innovative vowels of
194: Muduga are the product of two related developments: the retraction of front vowels before
195: retroflex consonants and /r/; and the fronting of back vowels before alveolar and palatal
196: consonants (except /r/ and /j/). We discuss each of these developments in turn below.
